styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a whole building like the references, so the kind matches. Its outlines are tinted dark blue-grey, brown and olive rather than neutral black (0% near-neutral edge pixels), which fits the Beodeul approach. The wall plaster speckle and the dark tile awnings with scallop marks show real texture. Three things keep it below the references. (1) The material ramps are shallow: the rooftop parapet and panels, the AC unit, the balcony rail and the door panels each use about 3-4 steps, against about 6 on the reference roofs. (2) 17% of its pixels sit in flat 5x5 blocks, mostly the rooftop slab and window or door panels, while both references measure 0%. (3) It has 9 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is slightly lower. The smooth modern surfaces read cleaner and flatter than the grainy, per-tile-highlighted references, and since the brief says to fail when in doubt, I fail it.

styleAnswer.evidence: The outlines are tinted: dark blue-grey beside the slate eaves and a dark olive-brown beside the plaster walls. The measured 0% neutral dark edge pixels agrees, so this is not a sticker outline. The shading and texture are thinner than the references. The rooftop parapet is a large grey slab with only panel lines. The doors, sash windows and balcony railing are close to flat two- or three-tone fills. The slate canopies have about 3-4 steps with little per-tile highlighting, where the references have per-tile highlights and scallops across 5-6 steps. The plaster speckle is the one real texture, but it is sparse and low contrast. The measured 17% near-flat coverage compares with 0% for both references. Visible tones per tile (9) are slightly under the references (12 and 10), and total colours are far lower (49 against 185 and 66). The piece is tidy and well structured, but it would look flatter and more plain-fill than the Beodeul houses beside them.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a whole building, so the kind matches, but it is a modern flat-roof house rather than a tiled-roof one. Its outlines are tinted: 0% of dark edge pixels are neutral, and they lean blue-grey beside the awnings and brown beside the doors. That part is fine. The measured facts are mixed. Visible tones per tile are 9, against 12 and 10 for the references, so that is near-equal. Near-flat coverage is 17%, against 0% for both references, and the picture agrees. The rooftop parapet panels and the grey wall are large flat grey areas with only thin seam lines. The doors, the sashes and the balcony rail are also mostly single flat tones. The plaster speckle on the walls and the awning tile rows show some texture. Even so, the awnings and parapet have only about 3-4 lightness steps, where the references reach about 6 on the roof tiles, timber and stone, each shaded tile by tile. Overall it reads cleaner, flatter and more vector-like than the Beodeul pieces, so I would not accept it beside them.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a whole building, so it matches the reference kind. The main weakness is shallow shading and flat areas. The rooftop slab and parapet are mostly flat grey with only thin panel lines. The blue-grey awning tiles show about 3-4 steps and the speckled plaster walls only 2-3, against about 6 steps on the references' tile roofs. The doors and window glass are also largely flat blocks.
